Q: Subfile WRITE fails with CPF5021 (status 9N / extended status 831D), even on a minimal test program A:

Found the root cause — posting here in case it helps someone else.

The DDS used negated indicators for the subfile display keywords:

     A N31                                  SFLDSP
     A N32                                  SFLDSPCTL
     A N33                                  SFLCLR

The "N" prefix means the keyword applies when the indicator is OFF, not ON. Every WRITE that set these indicators to "1" (thinking it activated display) was actually deactivating it. This compiled and ran without error for a long time, and only surfaced as CPF5066 ("SFLDSPCTL or SFLDSP option required for PUTGET") once the program tried to actually display/read the subfile control record.

Fix: remove the "N" prefix so the indicators mean what the program assumes:

     A  31                                  SFLDSP
     A  32                                  SFLDSPCTL
     A  33                                  SFLCLR

Two more things were required to get a clean minimal RPG repro working end-to-end:

  • SFILE(SFLREC:RRN) on the dcl-f, to link the RRN control field to the subfile record format (COBOL's RELATIVE KEY IS clause is the rough equivalent, but didn't surface the same class of error in COBOL — still investigating whether the same negated-indicator issue was the sole cause there too).
  • EXFMT instead of separate WRITE + READ on the control record.

Thanks to everyone on the IBM I community forum at pub400.com who helped narrow this down (Sam_L, Marco, PIKACHU) — cross-testing in RPG alongside COBOL, and getting more precise CPF messages at each step, was what eventually cracked it.

Q: How can I specify the Python version used to create a virtual environment? A:

Assuming that you have installed python3 or any desired version of Python (2.6, 2.7, 3.5, 3.6), Now while creating the virtual environment directly pass the python executable path. Hence here are few valid example

$ virtualenv new_p2_env # Creates a new default python environment (usually python 2)

$ virtualenv -p python3 new_p3_env # Creates a new default python3 (python3 must be a valid command i.e found in the PATH)

And last

# Directly point to any version of python binary, this can be even another virtualenv's bin/python. 
$ virtualenv -p /path/to/any/bin/python new_env

Q: Why can't borh be found? No ggplot? A:

Could be a syntax issue; see if this works:

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = dowell_raw, mapping = aes(x = factor(borh), y = bois, fill = factor(borh)) +
geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), color = "black") +
scale_fill_manual(values = c("coral", "skyblue"), name = "Treatment") +
labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Species Richness")

If you get the same error, you'll need to provide additional debugging details in order to find a solution, e.g. see https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example

Q: Content Security Policy causing 502 for WordPress admin login page A:

This is 2 years late so for the ones who are lost. Create a separate CSP policy for /wp-admin/ URLS since it uses inline scripts extensively, even in 2026. Use a relaxed policy for /wp-admin/ and keep a strict CSP for the front end.

Other ways to make up for the relaxed policy in your admin dashboard:

  1. wp-config.php
// prevents theme/plugin editing from the dashboard
define( 'DISALLOW_FILE_EDIT', true ); 
// prevents administrators from injecting arbitrary HTML
define( 'DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML', true );
define( 'WP_AUTO_UPDATE_CORE', 'minor' );
define( 'FORCE_SSL_ADMIN', true );

  1. Restrict /wp-admin/ access to specific IP addresses if you have a static IP via server level config

  2. Monitor the /wp-admin/admin-ajax.php endpoint, which is often targeted by bots through WP Activity Log plugin

  3. Really look over your file permission and enact ownership hardening

  4. Disable any access to wp-admin on server level configuration (i.e., .htaccess, nginx, etc).

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
RewriteEngine On
RewriteBase /
RewriteRule ^wp-admin/includes/ - [F,L]
RewriteRule !^wp-includes/ - [S=3]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/[^/]+\.php$ - [F,L]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/js/tinymce/langs/.+\.php - [F,L]
RewriteRule ^wp-includes/theme-compat/ - [F,L]
</IfModule>

Q: Double Free Vulnerability A:

No. s1 is not actually deleted from memory immediately. Rust simply marks s1 as invalid after the move. The compiler will not let you use s1 again, so safe Rust code cannot access that old pointer. When the variables go out of scope, only s2 frees the heap memory, which prevents a double free.

Example:

let s1 = String::from("Hello");
let s2 = s1;
// println!("{}", s1); // compile error
println!("{}", s2);    // Works

Here, s1 still exists as a variable, but it is no longer valid to use. Only s2 owns the string and will free the memory.

After this line:

let s2 = s1;

the memory looks like this:

Stack: s1: INVALID (cannot be used anymore) 
s2: pointer ----> Heap: "hello"

The important point is, the bits that represented s1 may still physically exist on the stack, but the Rust compiler treats s1 as moved.

Since the compiler prevents any access through s1, no safe Rust code can use that old pointer.

When s1 goes out of scope, Rust also knows not to call drop on it. Only s2 owns the heap allocation.

So there is only one owner, which prevents a double free.

Additionally, in safe Rust, you cannot obtain or use the old pointer after ownership has moved. However, in unsafe Rust, you can manually work with raw pointers:

let p = s1.as_ptr();

Raw pointers are not checked by the compiler.

That's why unsafe exists, it tells Rust:

"I know what I'm doing."

Unsafe means the responsibility is now yours.
